theme: I will sing of steadfast love and justice, David’s royal vow
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 101. David describes the kind of king he intends to be. Read it as a vow, and ask how it applies to anyone who has influence over others.
settingTheScene: Psalm 101 is a psalm of David, and it reads like a king’s inaugural pledge. He promises to rule with integrity, to avoid evil in his house, and to remove the wicked from the city. In the sequence of this unit, it comes after the temple is built and before the story of Solomon’s downfall. David’s vow stands in contrast to what Solomon will become.
observation: “I will sing of steadfast love and justice; to you, O LORD, I will make music” (v. 1).
“I will ponder the way that is blameless. Oh when will you come to me? I will walk with integrity of heart within my house” (v. 2).
“I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless” (v. 3).
“The one who has a haughty look and an arrogant heart I will not endure” (v. 5).
“I will look with favor on the faithful in the land, that they may dwell with me; he who walks in the way that is blameless shall minister to me” (v. 6).
“No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who utters lies shall continue before my eyes” (v. 7).
“Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked in the land” (v. 8).
“Cutting off all the evildoers from the city of the LORD” (v. 8).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with praise, not boasting. “I will sing of steadfast love and justice.” The twin themes of God’s own character become the foundation of David’s kingship. A king must reflect both love and justice. If either is missing, the rule fails.

The heart of the psalm is the integrity of the king’s own life. “I will walk with integrity of heart within my house.” Before David concerns himself with the nation, he concerns himself with the household. Private character comes first. A person’s integrity is tested where no one sees. “I will not set before my eyes anything that is worthless.” It is a commitment to guard what he looks at, an important thought for a man who fell through what he saw from his roof.

David then describes the kind of people he will have around him. He will not tolerate slander or arrogance. He will look for the faithful and honor them. A leader’s choice of associates shapes his rule. He will not let deceit dwell in his house.

The language of the closing verse may seem harsh, “Morning by morning I will destroy all the wicked,” but it refers to the king’s duty to administer justice, to purge evil from the community. The “morning by morning” recalls the daily court sessions held at the city gate.

We know that David did not live up to this vow. His sin with Bathsheba, his failure with his sons, and the rest of the story show that he fell short. And Solomon, who inherited the throne, would let deceit, idolatry, and compromise into his house. The psalm stands as an ideal that no human king achieved. It is an unfulfilled vow waiting for the king who would.
connection: Jesus is the king whose life matches this vow. He walked in the way that is blameless (Hebrews 4:15), and he will one day remove all evil from his kingdom (Matthew 13:41; Revelation 21:27). He looks with favor on the faithful (Matthew 25:21). Paul says that Christians should guard their eyes and hearts (Philippians 4:8). 1 John 2:16 warns about “the desires of the eyes.”
application:
Make a small vow like David’s about what you will not set before your eyes.

Reflect on how your integrity at home compares with your public self.

Consider who you allow near you as friends and advisers.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you walk with integrity at home.
Ask him to guard what you set before your eyes.
Confess where you have fallen short, and ask for help.
